newsitem.title: USA: Sears to refund payments of certain debtors.
newsitem.headline: Sears to refund payments of certain debtors.

text.p: Sears, Roebuck and Co said Thursday it had filed a motion in U.S. Bankruptcy Court for the District of Massachusetts to refund payments received from certain of its credit card debtors who have filed Chapter 7 bankruptcy.
A Sears spokesman said the credit card holders filed for bankruptcy but arranged some payment plan -- or "debt reaffirmation" -- with Sears.
Sears said the debt reaffirmations were not filed as required under the Bankruptcy Code.

Debt reaffirmations allow a debtor who is filing for bankruptcy to make payments to certain creditors in an effort to preserve his credit standing. Debt reaffirmations must be filed with the bankruptcy court in order to be valid.
Sears said it had exercised "flawed legal judgment" in the execution and handling of certain debt reaffirmations.
It said senior management last week directed that all reaffirmations must be filed in a timely fashion.
It said that on Wednesday it initiated a voluntary plan to refund payments made by certain debtors.
Sears said it is in the early stages of assessing the cost of the plan but that it may have a material effect on 1997 earnings.
Under the plan, Sears said, it will return amounts collected under reaffirmation agreements that were not filed with the bankruptcy court, including principal and finance charges with interest.
It said it has discussed its plan with the office of the Massachusetts Attorney General and the U.S. Bankruptcy Trustee for Region One, which includes Massachusetts.

To implement its plan, Sears said it will identify debtors whose reaffirmation agreements were not filed properly from 1992 to date. Until repayments can be made, the company said it will cease sending billing statements and assessing interest charges to former debtors who signed the reaffirmation agreements in question.
Sears said it has received documents relating to a class action lawsuit filed in the Bankruptcy Court of Massaschusetts that relate to these issues.
It said it had retained the services of Professor Lawrence King of the New York University School of Law to review its procedures with regard to the reaffirmation agreements.
